claims: Productivity is output per unit of input on a stated measurement basis.
definition
Total production can rise while productivity falls if the relevant input rises proportionately more than output.
comparison
Labour productivity can be measured as output divided by workers or by labour hours, with the denominator stated.
definition
Comparable productivity measures require a consistent output definition, quality basis, input unit and period.
factual
Training, suitable equipment, maintenance, organisation and motivation can improve productive efficiency when they reduce resources needed per satisfactory output.
causal
A productivity improvement increases satisfactory output for a given input or reduces input for a given satisfactory output.
definition
Information technology uses electronic systems to process, store or communicate information.
definition
Suitable information technology can reduce errors, repeated work and delays, but training, reliability and task fit affect the productivity result.
causal
HIV is a virus affecting the immune system; AIDS is an advanced stage of HIV infection, and effective treatment can help people remain healthy.
definition
Illness and caring-related absence can interrupt work and reduce output or increase replacement requirements; these effects depend on health and support rather than HIV status alone.
causal
Health support and access to effective treatment can help preserve continuity and skills; living with HIV does not establish inability to work productively.
evaluative

CU-6145-5.2:
Productivity is output per unit of input on a stated basis. Production tells us how much output is created, while productivity relates it to the resources used. More output can be useful without proving more efficient use of an input. If a workshop raises weekly output from 100 to 120 items while increasing labour hours from 50 to 80, output rises but items per labour hour fall from two to 1.5. The denominator changes the interpretation. A comparison omitting input is incomplete.

Name both sides of the ratio. Items per worker per week and items per labour hour are different measures. A worker count can hide differences in hours, so labour hours can give a more suitable basis where shifts differ. Quality also matters: producing more defective items is not necessarily a gain in satisfactory output. If the data specify completed acceptable units, use those consistently. Productivity is not a synonym for the speed of an individual worker or a measure of personal worth. Equipment, materials, organisation and working conditions can all influence the output achieved from labour.

Choose the denominator that matches the question. Comparing teams with equal headcounts can be useful when their hours are also equal, while a change in shift length requires more detail. If one measure is items per worker per month and another items per hour, they cannot be ranked directly without conversion data. The input unit is part of the result, rather than a label added after the calculation. A number such as four without packs per labour hour would leave its meaning unclear.

For an invented lunch-packing team, 480 satisfactory packs are produced in 120 labour hours. Labour productivity is 480 divided by 120, or four packs per labour hour. After a change, 540 packs are produced in the same hours, giving 4.5 per labour hour. The increase is 0.5 pack per hour, or 12.5 percent relative to the initial four. This figure describes output per labour hour; it is not a claim that total cost fell by exactly 12.5 percent or that profit rose by that amount.

Suppose instead the second output required 150 labour hours. Productivity would be 3.6 packs per hour, lower than the initial four despite greater production. This counterexample shows why total output is insufficient. An independent check multiplies the ratio by input: 3.6 packs per hour times 150 hours returns 540 packs. That confirms the arithmetic, while interpretation explains why a larger denominator changed the comparison. When drawing conclusions, hold the product and quality definition consistent and identify whether a change in staffing, equipment or organisation is also present. The ratio records an outcome; it does not by itself isolate which influence caused it.

Product mix can affect a count as well. A simple job and a complex repair may each count as one, despite requiring different resources. If the mix changes, a jobs-per-hour comparison may reflect the changed tasks. Use the quality and output definitions specified in the exercise and explain this limitation when relevant. The numerical examples deliberately hold satisfactory pack quality constant, allowing a clear comparison. A percentage ratio change then compares the new productivity with the old productivity, rather than dividing by total output.

A productivity improvement increases satisfactory output for a given input or reduces input for a given satisfactory output. Training can reduce mistakes and time spent repeating work. Suitable equipment can assist tasks that are difficult or slow manually. Maintenance can reduce breakdowns. Better layout and scheduling can reduce waiting or unnecessary movement. Motivation and clear communication may improve cooperation or retention. Each explanation needs a mechanism connecting the change to resources used per acceptable output, rather than a vague statement that workers become better.

At an invented frame workshop, moving frequently used tools nearer the work area can reduce searching time. If the saved time is used to complete more satisfactory frames with the same labour hours, measured labour productivity rises. Buying equipment without using it effectively would not establish that result. Training and reorganisation also use resources during implementation, so immediate output may be disrupted before later gains appear. Compare a suitable period and avoid assuming a possible gain is already achieved. Improvements can involve complementary changes: a new tool may need training and reliable materials to work well. A firm should identify the obstacle first, then choose a response suited to the task and check the actual ratio afterwards.

A maintenance example illustrates the difference between a mechanism and a result. Servicing a machine may reduce lost production time. If workers spend fewer hours waiting and complete more acceptable units in the same paid hours, labour productivity improves. If the time saved is offset by another bottleneck, the measured gain may be smaller or absent. Record what actually changes, including implementation time, before claiming the intervention achieved its aim. This makes the explanation testable using the relevant process and ratio data.
Information technology and the work process

Information technology uses electronic systems to process, store or communicate information. Its productivity effect depends on what problem it solves. An invented delivery service using a shared booking record may reduce repeated data entry and conflicting instructions. Staff spend less time correcting mistakes, allowing more completed deliveries for the same administrative hours. A stock record may help a workshop identify missing inputs earlier, reducing idle time. The mechanism is better information flow, rather than the presence of a computer by itself.

There are costs and limits. Staff need skills, accurate input data and reliable access. A poorly designed system may create duplicate tasks rather than remove them. Downtime can interrupt operations and a mismatch between the software and the job can waste resources. The effect should therefore be evaluated using completed satisfactory work and the relevant inputs over a fair period. A shorter booking time does not prove total delivery productivity increased if the same bottleneck remains elsewhere. Do not count a technical feature as an economic gain without explaining its consequence. This links to factor substitution in 5.1: electronic systems can change tasks and skill requirements rather than simply remove all need for people.

Compare an intended improvement with an observed one. A system proposal may promise fewer errors, but adoption alone does not establish that promise was met. Evidence could include time spent correcting orders, completed satisfactory jobs and the input hours used across comparable periods. An economic evaluation also compares the resources spent on implementation with the resulting benefits, while keeping that financial question distinct from the narrower productivity ratio. Both can matter without being identical measures of success.

The syllabus also asks about the effects of HIV and AIDS on productivity. HIV and AIDS are not interchangeable terms: HIV affects the immune system and AIDS describes an advanced stage of the infection. Effective treatment and care can support health, so a person’s HIV status alone does not establish low productivity or inability to work. The [World Health Organization explanation](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/hiv-aids) and [NIH basic facts](https://hivinfo.nih.gov/understanding-hiv/fact-sheets/hiv-and-aids-basics) support this distinction. The economic analysis concerns health-related disruption and the conditions that can reduce it, rather than assumptions about individuals.

Where illness causes absence or reduces the time someone can work, production can be interrupted. A firm may need cover, recruitment or training, and experienced knowledge can be difficult to replace. Caring responsibilities may also affect available hours. These mechanisms concern changes in labour availability and continuity. Lower total output is not enough to prove lower output per actual labour hour: the input may also have fallen. State which measure is being discussed and avoid silently switching between production and productivity.

Supportive arrangements, access to care and retaining trained staff can help maintain continuity. Their effects depend on actual circumstances and implementation; no treatment outcome or individual work capacity should be inferred from a group label. In an invented firm where employees can attend care appointments and tasks are covered through clear scheduling, fewer avoidable interruptions may protect output and skills. The economic reasoning is conditional, without inventing absence figures or attributing an employee’s behaviour to a diagnosis. This connects to labour supply and skills in topic 4.2 and employment in 7.2. A complete explanation identifies the initial disruption, the input or process affected and the possible consequence, while recognising that prevention, treatment and workplace support can change the outcome.

cards: Define productivity.
Output per unit of input on a stated measurement basis.
Definition: output/input 1; qualifier: specified input or basis 1.
Identify the denominator in packs per labour hour.
Labour hours (1).
Characteristic: labour hours, 1.
Explain why production rising from 100 to 120 units need not show higher productivity when labour hours rise from 50 to 80.
Output per hour falls from two to 1.5 (1), so the larger output uses proportionately more labour input (1).
Context: stated output/hours; reasoning: ratio comparison 1; result: productivity falls 1.
Define labour productivity measured per hour.
Satisfactory output divided by labour hours used in the stated period.
Meaning: output/labour input 1; qualifier: hours and period basis 1.
Calculate labour productivity for 480 satisfactory packs produced in 120 labour hours.
Formula: output/labour hours. Working: 480/120 = 4. Answer: four packs per labour hour.
Formula and working shown for learning; answer/unit four packs per labour hour earns the single result mark.
Explain a change from 480 packs in 120 labour hours to 540 packs in 120 hours, with quality unchanged.

Productivity rises from four to 4.5 packs per hour. The same labour input produces 60 extra packs, so output per hour increases by 0.5, or 12.5 percent. This does not itself establish an equal percentage profit gain.
Relationship: higher output/input 1; evidence: four to 4.5 and 12.5 percent 1; explanation: same hours and no profit inference 2.
Explain why worker counts alone may give an unfair productivity comparison when one team works longer shifts.
The same headcount can supply different labour hours (1), so output per worker may reflect time differences rather than equal-input performance (1).
Context: unequal shifts; reasoning: hours differ 1; result: common input basis needed 1.
Define a productivity improvement.
More satisfactory output from a given input, or less input for a given satisfactory output.
Definition: ratio improves 1; distinguishing feature: output or input held comparable 1.
Explain how appropriate training can improve productivity.
Initial change: workers learn a more effective method (1); fewer mistakes or repeated tasks allow more satisfactory output from the same input (1).
Initial change 1; mechanism/effect: less rework raises output/input 1.
Explain how placing tools nearer an invented workbench could improve labour productivity.
Less time is used searching or walking (1), so the same labour hours can produce more satisfactory items if the saved time supports production (1).
Context: workbench; reasoning: less wasted time 1; result: conditional output/hour gain 1.
Define information technology.
Electronic systems used to process, store or communicate information.
Meaning: electronic systems 1; qualifier: information processing/storage/communication 1.
Explain how a shared booking record can affect an invented delivery firm’s productivity.
Initial change: staff use one consistent record (1); reduced repeated entry or conflicting instructions can free input time for completed work (1).
Initial change 1; mechanism/effect for firm: fewer errors/repetition can improve completed output/input 1.
Explain why installing software alone does not prove higher productivity in an invented workshop.
Training, reliable data and task fit may be missing (1), so the system may fail to reduce resources per satisfactory output (1).
Context: installation; reasoning: implementation conditions 1; result: no demonstrated ratio gain 1.
Define the distinction between HIV and AIDS relevant to the syllabus topic.
HIV is the virus affecting the immune system; AIDS is an advanced stage of HIV infection.
Meaning and distinguishing feature: virus versus advanced stage, 1 each; no inference of work capacity from status.
Explain how illness-related absence can disrupt a firm’s production without assuming every person living with HIV is unable to work.
Initial change: actual illness reduces available work time (1); missing skills or cover needs may interrupt output, while health and support determine the effect rather than status alone (1).
Initial change: illness-related absence 1; mechanism/effect for firm: interrupted time/skills under stated conditions 1.
Explain why support for access to effective care may help an invented firm retain productive skills.
Support can help employees maintain health and continuity (1), reducing avoidable disruption or replacement needs rather than treating a diagnosis as inability (1).
Context: care access; reasoning: continuity support 1; result: skills retained/less disruption as a possibility 1.
performance: The invented Fresh Pack team produces 480 satisfactory packs in 120 labour hours. After training and a tool-layout change, it produces 540 packs in the same hours with unchanged quality. Its new electronic stock record has occasional downtime. No total cost data is supplied. (a) Describe three relevant features (6). (b) Examine what can be concluded about productivity and its causes (7). (c) Suggest how the firm should evaluate further improvement (7).

(a) Output rises by 60 packs. Labour hours remain 120. Quality is unchanged, while the electronic system is not fully reliable. (b) Output per labour hour rises from four to 4.5, a 12.5 percent increase. Training and reduced tool searching can help explain the process, but both changed together so the exact contribution of each is not isolated. Downtime can offset information benefits. No equal percentage cost or profit gain is established. (c) Track satisfactory output and hours consistently, note errors and downtime, and compare suitable periods after staff learn the system. Investigate the specific bottleneck before more spending. The judgement should use actual ratio and complete cost evidence, retaining the quality standard rather than rewarding more defective output.

Context: Fresh Pack. Parts/allocation: (a) output, hours, quality/reliability, 2 each = 6. (b) ratio evidence 2, mechanism 2, attribution/downtime 2, profit boundary 1 = 7. (c) comparable measurement 2, targeted investigation 2, quality/cost-based judgement 3 = 7.

(a) Define productivity (2). (b) Define labour productivity per hour (2). (c) Explain why more production need not mean more productivity (2). (d) Explain how training can improve the ratio (2). (e) Explain how maintenance can help (2). (f) Explain one condition for IT gains (2). (g) Explain why HIV status alone does not establish productivity (2). (h) Explain why illness-related output loss need not equal a measured fall in output per actual hour (2).

(a) Output per unit of input. (b) Output divided by labour hours for a stated period. (c) Inputs may rise proportionately more. (d) Less error/rework can raise satisfactory output from the same time. (e) Fewer breakdowns reduce lost time. (f) Task fit and trained users are needed to avoid adding errors or repetition. (g) Health and support vary; effective treatment can help people remain healthy. (h) Actual labour hours may also fall, so the ratio must be calculated rather than inferred from output alone.

Parts/allocation and precision: eight at 2 each. (a) output + input; (b) labour hours + period; (c) output rise + larger input; (d) skill + rework mechanism; (e) breakdown reduction + productive time; (f) condition + mechanism; (g) individual conditions + no status-only inference; (h) output/input distinction.

The invented North Repairs firm adopts an electronic job record while providing staff training. Some workers also need scheduled time for healthcare appointments. Managers propose measuring performance solely by the number of jobs completed, without recording labour hours or job quality. (a) Define information technology (2). (b) Explain two ways the job record might affect productivity (4). (c) Explain how training, reliable implementation and health support could affect productive continuity (7). (d) Discuss whether the proposed measure is adequate (7).

(a) Electronic systems processing, storing or communicating information. (b) Shared information can reduce repeated entry and errors. Poor implementation or downtime can instead consume time and delay jobs. (c) Training helps staff use records correctly, while reliability prevents system interruptions. Healthcare access and sensible cover can support continuity and retention of skills. Actual effects depend on needs and implementation; an appointment or health status alone does not establish low work capacity. These processes can reduce avoidable disruption but require an actual output/input comparison. (d) Jobs completed measure production, not productivity alone. Hours and quality may differ, so higher count can coexist with lower satisfactory jobs per hour. Record comparable quality-adjusted output and labour input over an appropriate period, alongside relevant process information. The proposed measure is useful as one output record but inadequate for the productivity conclusion.

Context: North Repairs. Parts/allocation: (a) electronic system 1, information function 1. (b) positive and negative mechanism 2 each = 4. (c) training/reliability 3, health/cover continuity 3, condition/ratio distinction 1 = 7. (d) output value 2, missing input/quality 2, supported measurement judgement 3 = 7.

Evaluate whether an invented processor should judge new technology successful solely because total monthly output rose, when labour hours, quality and complete implementation costs are not reported (9).

For: greater output may indicate useful capacity or a faster process and provides a reason to investigate gains. Against: input may have increased more, quality may have fallen and training or downtime may use resources. A technology purchase can also change tasks without removing bottlenecks. Judgement: compare satisfactory output per consistent input over a suitable period and examine complete relevant costs. The condition for a productivity claim is a better output/input ratio on a comparable quality basis, not higher production alone. Financial success requires further cost and revenue evidence.

Argument for: potential productive improvement developed, up to 4. Argument against: input/quality/implementation limits developed, up to 4. Judgement: distinct ratio and financial-evidence condition, 1. Total 9.
judgements: HIV and AIDS distinction and treatment context checked with WHO/NIH on 28 October 2026. Economic discussion is conditional and avoids status-based inferences or medical treatment advice.
Output per actual labour hour is distinguished from total output affected by absence.
